events.title: Mansfield Herbert opens an Underground Railroad station in South Trenton
events.description: A Tribune profile of his son reports that from 1843 until the Civil War, Mansfield Herbert's house in South Trenton was the principal Underground Railroad station between Philadelphia and New Brunswick. Herbert had escaped slavery at 14 and later bought freedom for himself, his father, and his sister for more than $3,000.

events.title: Alfred P. Smith writes to President Lincoln against colonization
events.description: While working as a reporter for the Paterson Guardian, Alfred P. Smith of Saddle River sent President Abraham Lincoln a letter criticizing the proposal to colonize freed slaves abroad.

events.title: Smith starts a job-printing business in Saddle River
events.description: After his father died, Alfred P. Smith started a job-printing business in Saddle River. The 1987 Ridgewood News gives no address for the shop. He later launched his own newspaper partly to advertise it.

events.title: R. Henri Herbert founds The Weekly Sentinel in Trenton
events.description: Herbert founded The Weekly Sentinel in 1880 and ran it for three years before selling it to Colonel E. C. Stahl, who merged it into The Trenton Herald. Herbert had already worked as business manager of The New-Jersey State Republican in Plainfield and as an editorial writer for The Daily State Sentinel and The Daily Free Press in Trenton.

events.title: Alfred P. Smith publishes the first issue of A.P. Smith's Paper
events.description: The 1987 Ridgewood News says Smith printed the 9-by-15-inch sheets himself in a house on East Allendale Road in Saddle River from May 1881 until July 1901; The Record dates the paper's start to 1881. He wrote, edited, printed, translated, and distributed it alone, and the paper was later renamed The Landscape. The press purchase is not part of this event: The Record puts it in the late 1870s, several years before the paper, and separates the two acts. Sources conflict on the first issue. The 1987 Ridgewood News and the 1991 Record give May 1881; the 1993 Sunday News dates the first issue to June 1882 and treats 'A. P. Smith's Paper' as an earlier predecessor title.

events.title: Herbert serves as NJ commissioner of colored exhibits at the New Orleans Exposition
events.description: In 1884-85 R. Henri Herbert served as New Jersey commissioner of the Department of Colored Exhibits at the New Orleans Exposition, then returned to Trenton to manufacture cigars.

events.title: The World reprints a New Jersey Trumpet editorial
events.description: Joseph Pulitzer's New York morning paper The World printed a standalone item headed 'A Roaring Jersey Negro Editor,' credited '[From the New Jersey Trumpet-Negro Organ.]'. It sits below the paper's 'SQUIBS FROM THE SQUIBOBS' column, set off by its own printer's rule, rather than inside it. The item is fully legible and is a reprint from the Trumpet, not a report about an unidentified paper. It reads in part: 'The Southern white man has the same contempt, hatred and enmity to the black man to-day as he had before the "wah." ... Better a thousand times we should be exterminated than surrender one single right so dearly purchased.' The file slug and the reading log call the paper the Evening World; the masthead and running head both read The World.

events.title: Col. William Murrell of the New Jersey Trumpet receives a federal commission
events.description: The Washington Bee reported that Col. Wm. Murrell, editor of the New Jersey Trumpet, received his commission for an Interior Department appointment on Wednesday, May 15, 1889. A gossip item on the same page said the Bee would take over the Trumpet's subscribers.

events.title: The Washington Bee reports Murrell will enter his federal office on May 25
events.description: The Washington Bee of May 18, 1889 reported that Murrell had received his commission on Wednesday and 'will enter upon the duties of his new office on the 25th.' A May 18 issue cannot witness May 25, and no later source in the reading base confirms that he took office. This event records the announcement, not the taking of office.

events.title: Smith campaigns for paved roads in Saddle River and wins the vote
events.description: Smith used The Landscape to push for paving Saddle River's roads. The source quotes his macadam argument tagged '(April, 1891)' and then reports that the vote to pave carried and $2,000 was appropriated, without giving a date for the vote. A separate quote tagged '(June, 1891)' predicts Bergen County's suburban growth, and an intervening quote is tagged '(Feb. 1890),' so the column is not in chronological order and does not date the campaign beyond the single April 1891 quote.

events.title: Mass meeting at Marrow's Hall protests Asbury Park's pavilion color line
events.description: Black residents met at Marrow's Hall in West Park to protest signs on James A. Bradley's Asbury Park pavilions barring Black patrons. Col. William Murrell, editor of the New Jersey Trumpet, spoke from the platform. Bradley arrived later and defended the policy as a private property right. The two papers do not disagree about attendance: both print the same sentence, and the Shore Press column is tagged 'From Saturday's DAILY.' above it. The sentence gives two sequential counts, about 100 people assembled at 8 o'clock and a crowd of nearly 500 once word spread.

events.title: The Shore Press notes the first issue of the New Jersey Trumpet's Monmouth edition
events.description: On July 28, 1893 the Shore Press reported that the first issue of the Monmouth edition of the New Jersey Trumpet, Murrell's Newark-based Black weekly, had just reached its office, and that Rev. Fillmore Smith, D. D., edited the Monmouth edition. The notice gives no launch date, no editorial remit, and no place of editing, so this event is dated to the day the Shore Press noted the copy's arrival.

events.title: Smith editorializes against 'barbarism' in The Landscape
events.description: Smith wrote against racism in The Landscape, invoking Senator Sumner's 'Barbarism of Slavery' speech and arguing that daily barbarism 'would disgrace a nation of savages' still remained.

events.title: R. Henri Herbert circulates a letter urging Black voters to defeat James A. Bradley
events.description: Herbert wrote and circulated a public letter urging Black voters in Monmouth County to help defeat Bradley's state senate candidacy, citing Bradley's order the previous summer barring Black waiters from his Asbury Park band pavilion.

events.title: Herbert joins the NJ Republican State Committee as a consulting member
events.description: The state committee adopted a resolution naming Herbert a consulting member charged with securing the Black vote statewide for gubernatorial candidate John W. Griggs. He shared the work with Charles R. Robinson, the Black committee member from Camden.

events.title: The New-York Tribune profiles Herbert and documents his newspaper career
events.description: A New Jersey news page sketch, 'A Noted Colored Leader,' laid out Herbert's biography: born in Trenton in 1857, in newspapers from boyhood, founder of The Weekly Sentinel, and the organizer who unified Black Republican voters in Mercer County behind Gov. Griggs.

events.title: The Landscape ceases when Alfred P. Smith dies
events.description: Smith stopped publishing in July 1901. The Record's account says the paper ceased in July 1901 and Smith died four months later at age 69. The 1993 Sunday News agrees on age 69: it quotes him writing 'at the age of 65, four years before his death in 1901.' The Ridgewood News says the paper ceased when he died, in July 1901, so the sources still conflict on whether the paper stopped before Smith died or with him. The Hackensack Republican eulogized him as 'a conspicuous figure and a power among the men of his race.'

events.title: Fire damages the Echo's press room in Long Branch
events.description: The Monmouth Democrat reported that the Echo, a Black weekly published in Long Branch, was burned out by a fire believed to be of incendiary origin. Machinery and press room damage ran to several hundred dollars. The item noted the paper's first issue was edited by Rock & Howard.

events.title: The Echo moves from Long Branch to Red Bank
events.description: The Asbury Park Evening Press reported that The Echo, edited and published in the interest of the colored race in Long Branch by W. E. Rock for the past five years, had moved to Red Bank, where Editor Rock had purchased a home. The item says he 'wll help run an industrial school for his race at Red Bank' - he is a participant, not the principal. The clipping prints 'Rock' twice; the reading log's 'Rack' is a transcription error, and publication id 31 names him 'Rock, William E.'

events.title: R. Henri Herbert dies suddenly in a Trenton street
events.description: Herbert, a document clerk at the New Jersey State House and a leading Black Republican, was found dead in the middle of a street in Trenton. The New York Age gave the death page-one play.

events.title: R. Henri Herbert's funeral is held in Trenton
events.description: The New York Age of Thursday, October 21, 1909 carried a Trenton dateline of October 19 reporting that funeral services 'were held last Saturday' - October 16, 1909. Services were held at the late residence, 25 Lambertson street, at 1 o'clock and at Mt. Zion A. M. E. Church at 2 o'clock, Rev. H. B. Anderson officiating, and the remains were interred in Riverview Cemetery. Every element of the service is in Trenton; Newark appears only as the home city of some honorary pallbearers and of out-of-town friends. The honorary pallbearers named are mostly out of state: Fred R. Moore, George S. Douglas, D. S. Willie, Robert R. Willis, John T. Lewis and M. P. Launders of New York, Chris Perry of Philadelphia, and William S. Powell of Camden. The account is retrospective throughout, so there is no announcement-versus-report conflict to disclose. The article also reports memorial resolutions adopted by the Essex County Colored Republican Association.

events.title: The New York Age cites the Red Bank Echo in its press-comment column
events.description: The Age's editorial press-comment column ran a one-sentence summary of a Red Bank Echo item about a Baltimore man who had a five-inch horn removed from his forehead. It is a comment on what the Echo had itself cited, not reprinted copy and not a clippings column. Neighboring paragraphs comment on the Detroit Leader, the Christian Recorder, the Beaumont (Tex.) Monitor, the Galveston City Times, and the Norfolk Journal and Guide, which shows a small shore weekly being read across the national Black press.

events.title: The Ironsides Echo wins a Columbia scholastic press award
events.description: The Ironsides Echo, the monthly student paper of the New Jersey State Manual Training and Industrial School for Colored Youth in Bordentown, won second place among the technical and agricultural high schools in the grading of school papers announced by the Columbia University Scholastic Press Association. The gradings were said to represent 860 publications, from high schools, preparatory schools and academies. Leon Snead was the student editor. Gov. A. Harry Moore had no role: he appears only in a separate Atlantic County election-board item in the adjacent column of the same page.

events.title: The Afro-American reports the Newark Herald has ceased publication
events.description: A Washington edition item said the Newark Herald, described as New Jersey's only colored weekly, had stopped publishing after more than four years, and that editor Clark had moved his office out of the well-known Cotton Building. The same item predicted the paper would come back: 'while no statement has been made, it is expected that he will receive the necessary backing for its resumption.' The suspension was temporary. Volume 11 in 1938 is exactly what a 1928 first volume produces, and two mastheads state the 1928 start outright: the June 11, 1938 Newark Herald reads 'Entered as second class matter May 4, 1928 at the Post Office at Newark, N. J.' and the July 4, 1942 Herald News reads 'Established 1928 as Newark Herald.'

events.title: Third Ward protest returns a Black Douglass Park attendant to her job
events.description: A protesting group of Third Ward citizens led by Mrs. Elizabeth Mitchell, a prominent political leader, kept up the fight for the re-employment of the women dismissed as attendants at Douglass Park. Mrs. Carrie Bartee was placed back in her former position; Mrs. Grace Bell and Mrs. Dorothy Hynes were still out. The protest reached its height on Wednesday, May 4, when Attorney Roger M. Yancey called the situation to the members of the City Commission after Deputy Director Ernest Masini had refused to listen to a committee of colored leaders. The New Jersey Herald News covered it.

events.title: Kenneth Worde sues the Liberty Theatre in Elizabeth over Jim Crow pricing
events.description: Worde, a Summit political leader, filed a civil rights suit against Skouras Liberty Theatre Corp. over segregated seating and admission pricing at the Elizabeth theater. George M. Fieldman was his attorney. The story ran in the left column of the New Jersey Herald News front page of May 21, 1938, below the banner 'LANDLORD BARS ALL NEGRO GUESTS' and a Satchel Paige strip head; it did not lead the page.

events.title: The New Jersey Herald News publishes Vol. 1, No. 3
events.description: The third issue of the new Newark weekly carried Melvin B. Johnson as managing editor, Oliver W. Brown as business manager, and H. B. Kelley as advertising director. Volume 1, Number 3 on May 21, 1938 places the paper's first issue in early May 1938.

events.title: Two Newark Black weeklies publish the same day and are bound together
events.description: A single archive scan holds The Newark Herald (Vol. 11, No. 18) and the New Jersey Herald News (Vol. 1, No. 6), both dated Saturday, June 11, 1938. The Herald ran under Merrill Biddle as president and Julius J. Adams as managing editor; the Herald News carried the ownership line 'Owned and Published by New Jersey Negroes' beside its nameplate. The pair confirms two competing Black weeklies operated in Newark at once before their later merger. The June 11 reading log renders three masthead names incorrectly. Five other logs in this batch read 'Julius J. Adams' (NewarkHerald19380618a, 19380702a, 19380709a, 19380716a, 19380723a) against the log's 'Julius X. Adams', and one other log in the batch reads 'Melvin B. Johnson' (NewJerseyHeraldNews19380521a) against the log's 'Melvin R. Johnson'. The masthead itself, read at high resolution, gives 'MERRILL BIDDLE ... President / JULIUS J. ADAMS ... Managing Editor / E. SWEENEY JONES ... Business Manager', so the log's 'F. Sweeney Jones' is a third OCR error.

events.title: Black leaders are refused service at Newark's Novelty Bar & Grill
events.description: The New Jersey Herald News reported that five prominent members of the race were refused service at the Novelty Bar & Grill, 220 Market St., Newark: Mr. Harold Lett, executive secretary of the New Jersey Urban League and a member of the Newark Housing Authority; Mrs. J. B. Parks, wife of Dr. J. B. Parks; Miss Alene Simpkins, social worker of the Urban League; Dr. William Kinchelow; and Miss Carolyn Hilliard, recreation supervisor at Morton Street School. The headline read 'Leading Citizens Victim Of Jim Crow At Novelty Bar; Planning To Enter Suit' - the group was planning a suit, not petitioning a prosecutor. Robert F. Kearse's petition to the Union County prosecutor, printed on the same page, is a separate story about police protection for Vaux Hall merchants, and the assault on Anna Nash on the same page is an unrelated street-crime brief about an unknown assailant.

events.title: Long Branch adopts a beach ordinance aimed at Black non-residents and excursionists
events.description: The Newark Herald covered a Long Branch ordinance abolishing the leasing of city-owned beaches, which the paper said closed 'the last vestige of open bathing along the North Jersey beach front' to Negroes. The story concerns the Long Branch city beach front, not a place called North Long Branch. The paper stated the ordinance was 'aimed primarily at the Negroes visiting the city', and the June 11 issue lists a $3 fee for non-resident bathers against $1 each person, per season for residents. Local Black residents already used Dixon's Beach, and the fight was over being confined to it. The local Committee on Legal Redress and NAACP opposition was led by Rev. Jackson.

events.title: Arthur A. Schomburg dies in Brooklyn
events.description: The Newark Herald reported the death of Schomburg, curator of the Negro literature and history collection at the 135th Street branch of the New York Public Library.

events.title: Daniel Winge disappears from the Douglass-Harrison apartments
events.description: The Newark Herald reported that bank and insurance cashier Daniel Winge vanished from the Douglass-Harrison Apartments with a shortage of about $2,000, then mailed a letter from Grand Central pledging to return and tell all. June 3, 1938 is the postmark on that letter, not a documented disappearance date, so this event is dated to the Herald's first coverage. The read issues that carry the story are June 11 and July 2, 1938; the story returns on July 16 and July 23 (see evt-036 and evt-038). The June 18 and July 9, 1938 issues do not mention Winge.

events.title: Joe Louis knocks out Max Schmeling and gives $2,500 to the Urban League and NAACP
events.description: Both Newark weeklies built up and then covered the Yankee Stadium rematch, including Louis's training at Pompton Lakes with James Braddock and Gene Tunney. After the one-round win Louis donated $2,500 from the receipts to the Urban League and the NAACP.

events.title: James Weldon Johnson is killed in a Maine grade-crossing crash
events.description: Both The Newark Herald and the New Jersey Herald News led their July 2 issues with the death of the poet and former NAACP executive secretary, whose car was struck by a train near Wiscasset, Maine. His widow Grace Nail Johnson was injured. The Newark Herald eulogized him on its editorial page, and the Springfield Avenue branch library in Newark exhibited his books.

events.title: About 100,000 people attend the Weequahic Park Independence Day festival
events.description: The Newark Herald reported a crowd of roughly 100,000 at the Weequahic Park July 4 observance.

events.title: Daniel E. Winge is arrested and pleads guilty to embezzlement
events.description: The July 16, 1938 issue reported that Detective William J. Freary had arrested the former assistant manager of the Douglass-Harrison Apartments. Winge pleaded guilty, and the issue said sentencing was set for July 20.

events.title: The North Jersey Baptist Association parades through Newark's Third Ward
events.description: The association's Silver Jubilee parade honored Dr. L. K. Williams, president of the National Baptist Convention. Rev. J. H. Burks chaired the parade committee and Dr. C. T. Wilcher was re-elected moderator.

events.title: The Newark Herald reports Winge's sentencing; the Herald News prints a jailhouse confession
events.description: Page 1 of the July 23, 1938 Newark Herald (Vol. 11, No. 23) reported that Winge 'was sentenced to a term of from two to [two and a half years] of hard labor in the state prison Wednesday by Judge Daniel J. Brennen in General Sessions court.' The Wednesday before Saturday, July 23, 1938 is July 20, which matches the sentencing date the July 16 issue reported as set (evt-036), so the sentencing is datable from the issue itself. The sentencing and the jailhouse confession did not run alongside each other in one paper: the scan binds two weeklies together, and the confession is the banner lead of a separate front page, the New Jersey Herald News of the same week (Vol. 1, No. 12).

events.title: The Ku Klux Klan burns a cross at Fayson Lake near Butler
events.description: After a Black family moved into the Fayson Lake development, the Klan burned a cross and a mob stoned the cottage. The story ran on page 2 of the July 30, 1938 Newark Herald (Vol. 11, No. 24) under the head 'Hooded Mob Stirs Terror - Fiery Cross Burned in Front of House at Fayson Lake Development,' not on the front page. That week's front page carried the Dowd Natatorium closing, the Route 29 crash, the Federation 'Mammy' row, and Hoot Gibson's indictment.

events.title: 'The Duke Is Tops' opens at the National Theatre in Newark
events.description: The Ralph Cooper and Lena Horne film opened in Newark and was covered on the paper's entertainment pages alongside Apollo Theatre news and a reprinted Paul Robeson speech.

events.title: Elizabeth closes the Dowd Natatorium rather than desegregate it
events.description: A Negro delegation led by NAACP Elizabeth branch president Dr. William H. Brown, with attorney J. Leroy Jordan as spokesman, refused a segregated-hours compromise. The Elizabeth Recreation Commission voted to close the pool permanently for the season. The July 30, 1938 issue never names a drowning victim; its only related line is 'It is feared more drownings will take place as a result of the closing of the pool.' The drowning is documented in the previous week's issue, which reports that William (Bud) Jackson, 17, of 178 Front street, was drowned in the Staten Island Sound 'within 600 feet of the pool from which he was barred.'

events.title: A WPA official's 'Mammy' remark draws protest at the Bordentown women's convention
events.description: Mrs. Elizabeth C. Denny Van, state director of Women's and Professional Projects for the WPA, made a remark about 'Mammy' at the NJ State Federation of Colored Women's Clubs convention at Bordentown, and Mrs. Armeta H. Douglass objected. The Newark Herald made the exchange front-page news in its July 30, 1938 issue, which places the remark on 'last Wednesday.' The convention was printed in advance as running July 20, 21, 22 and 23, 1938, so its only Wednesday was July 20; July 27 falls after the convention closed. The July 23 issue's own line that the convention 'was opened July 15 for a five-day session' conflicts with the printed program, so the exact day is not settled.

events.title: Mrs. Ida Brown is elected president of the NJ State Federation of Colored Women's Clubs
events.description: Brown, of Jersey City, succeeded Mrs. Alice B. Arrington, who resigned to take a YWCA post in Baltimore. Federation founder Rev. Florence Randolph presided at the election in Bordentown.

events.title: The state commission reports systemic denial of rights to 200,000 Black New Jerseyans
events.description: The New Jersey Herald News front-paged the NJ State Temporary Commission on the Condition of the Urban Colored Population, chaired by Dr. Frank S. Hargraves, and demanded legislative and administrative action.

events.title: The paper calls the Baxter inquiry at Rutgers a whitewash
events.description: Ernest Baxter was barred by the University of Maryland. A committee of Essex County Assemblymen waited on Rutgers College officials about the barring, and colored citizens throughout the state branded that investigation a 'whitewash' precisely because no charge of racial discrimination had ever been made against the New Brunswick college. This is not a Rutgers admissions-bias case, and Rutgers was not accused and then exonerated. The New Jersey Herald News printed the charge on its March 11, 1939 front page under the head 'Baxter Case "Whitewashed"'.

events.title: The New Jersey Herald News launches a municipal investigative series and claims seniority
events.description: The March 11, 1939 issue (Vol. XII, No. 5) carried the masthead 'combined with THE NEWARK HERALD' and the billing 'New Jersey's Oldest Colored Weekly, Twelfth Year.' Its front page opened a multi-part series, 'Obstacles Faced By The Race In NEWARK,' introduced as 'the first of a series of facts to be published about the conditions affecting Negroes in various municipalities of New Jersey.' The installment ends on page 2 with the kicker '(NEXT WEEK: PATERSON)'. The only Jersey City item on that front page is an unrelated story about Dr. A. W. Johnson qualifying as a specialist. An editorial titled 'The Negro Press in New Jersey' positioned the paper inside a statewide network of Black papers.

events.title: The Jersey Guardian praises a Paterson college president as a foe of prejudice
events.description: The Paterson Evening News reported that The Jersey Guardian, a statewide newspaper for Black readers, published an article praising Dr. Herbert Spencer Robinson, president of the College of Paterson, who favored boycotts to fight segregation. The same page covered Robinson introducing NAACP field secretary William Pickens at a Paterson branch meeting.

events.title: The Ironsides Echo wins two more Columbia press awards
events.description: The May 7, 1940 issue of the Trenton Evening Times reported that the Bordentown Manual Training and Industrial School student paper had taken two second-place awards in Columbia University's 16th annual scholastic press contest, its second documented showing after 1932. The issue reports the awards as already made; it does not date the contest itself.

events.title: The FBI holds Glen Ridge conscientious objector Bill Sutherland
events.description: The New Jersey Herald News led its July 4 issue with Sutherland, held in Hackensack for refusing to report to a CCC camp in Coshocton, Ohio, and released on $500 bail.

events.title: The New Jersey Herald News runs 12 pages and claims to be the state's oldest colored weekly
events.description: The July 4, 1942 issue (15th Year, No. 26) described itself as 'New Jersey's oldest and only colored weekly of 12 pages or more' and published from 130 W. Kinney St., Newark. Frederick W. Martin was president of the Herald News Publishing Co. and Richard L. Martin secretary-treasurer. The address is not shared with the Newark Herald and is not evidence of the merger: the June 11, 1938 Newark Herald masthead gives 152 West Kinney St. and telephone MArket 3-0940, while the Herald News gives 130 West Kinney Street and MArket 2-9799 - different buildings on the same street.

events.title: William R. Jackson becomes the first Black member of the Newark Board of Education
events.description: Mayor Vincent Murphy named Jackson, executive secretary of the Court Street YMCA, to the board. The Herald News reported he was the first Black appointee in the board's 106-year history.

events.title: The New Jersey Afro-American publishes its 'Year of Great Negro Resistance to Hate Groups' issue
events.description: The issue featured the blinded Black veteran Isaac Woodard on its cover.

events.title: Melvin B. Johnson leaves the Black newspaper business for Republican politics
events.description: The Star-Ledger reported that Johnson, a former Negro newspaper publisher and editor, was in the newspaper field until 1946, when he left to work among Negro voters in Gov. Driscoll's gubernatorial campaign, and that he was then a public relations assistant in the N. J. Department of Labor. The item names no newspaper, so the departure is not attached to a specific title here; the Montclair weekly (publication 2) and the New Jersey Herald News (publication 16) are equally available candidates.

events.title: Johnson is named a prospective Newark City Commission candidate
events.description: The Star-Ledger listed Johnson, of 55 Somerset St., Newark, among prospective candidates for the May municipal election.

events.title: Johnson is announced as principal speaker at a West Side Republican club wind-up rally
events.description: The Asbury Park Sunday Press of November 6, 1949 announced that Melvin B. Johnson 'will be the principal speaker Monday night at the West Side Republican club's wind-up rally at the Reindeer Rest, Atkins avenue, at 9 o'clock,' with Mayor George A. Smock, 2d, and all candidates on the last pre-election program. This is the club's own wind-up rally, not a Driscoll rally; Johnson is a Driscoll campaign aide invited to speak. The item described him as a former editor and publisher of weekly newspapers at Montclair and Newark, employed by the migrant labor division of the New Jersey department of labor and industry. It dates his close association with Driscoll to 1946, when he left newspaper work for the Governor's first campaign, and places the minority-group adviser role after a later appointment, not in 1946. The source reports the November 7 rally as upcoming; it does not report that it was held.

events.title: Bronze Thrills publishes a Lakewood woman's life story
events.description: Emily Rodriquez of Lakewood, entering a Carmelite convent on June 12, 1960, wrote a book based on her life, 'Out of Darkness to Light,' scheduled for the July issue of Bronze Thrills.

events.title: MEDIC Enterprises incorporates in Newark
events.description: MEDIC Enterprises, Inc. (Minority, Economic, Development, Industrial and Cultural Enterprises) was founded and incorporated as a New Jersey non-profit in September 1968. Its own newsletter later told the story. The newsletter credits unnamed founders; Elvin R. Austin (president) and William A. Mercer (board chairman) are identified only by their 1971 roles, so neither is listed here as a founder.

events.title: MEDIC Press opens with donated letterpress equipment
events.description: MEDIC Enterprises founded MEDIC Press, Inc. in July 1969 with $9,000 of donated letterpress equipment. In ten months of 1970 the shop grossed close to $45,000 and acquired about $30,000 in fixed assets.

events.title: MEDIC News publishes its first issue and claims the Black press tradition
events.description: The eight-page Newark newsletter launched with an unsigned institutional statement headed 'FROM MEDIC,' written in the first person plural for the organization: 'We at MEDIC, have accepted the task of filling the city's information void, and we expect to fulfill it with as much austerity of purpose, accuracy and relevance as the black journals of the early 1800's provided for their communities.' The statement carries no byline. Carolyn Odom is named on the same page only as the editor to whom readers should address comments, so the framing is not attributable to her personally. The issue profiled MEDIC Press, board chairman William A. Mercer, and MEDIC-financed businesses, and covered Mayor Kenneth Gibson's economic development committee.

events.title: Newark holds its first annual Manpower Workshop-Conference
events.description: The April 23-24 conference at Ebony Manor, 100 Clinton Avenue, took up 'Newark's Manpower Needs: New Directions for the 70's,' with Clayton J. Cottrell, Cyril Tyson, and Sen. Harrison P. Williams as speakers. MEDIC News covered it in its launch issue.

events.title: The first National Black Political Convention meets in Gary, Indiana
events.description: A January 2022 Nubian News article on the announcement of a 2022 convention recaps the original: the first National Black Political Convention was held in Gary, Indiana, March 10-12, 1972, hosted by Gary mayor Richard Hatcher and organized with Amiri Baraka, Sr. and US Rep. Charles Diggs. The article names Ron Daniels as a key organizer who led a reparations demand, and Betty Shabazz and Coretta Scott-King among the attendees, and says the convention adopted the Gary Declaration. This is a 2022 retrospective account, not contemporaneous reporting.

events.title: Trenton State trustees vote to arm campus police over minority student opposition
events.description: The board voted 4-1 for a six-month trial arming patrolmen from September 1. The student government ardently opposed the move and was supported by the Minority Executive Council and Utimme Umana/La Voz Oculta, the weekly minority publication on campus. The administration, the 14 police officers, and The Signal, the student newspaper, favored arming the officers. The faculty senate was divided. The reading log for this clipping reverses The Signal's position; the printed page is the controlling source.

events.title: Ollie Stewart dies in Paris
events.description: Stewart, the first accredited Black war correspondent of World War II, reported for the New Jersey Afro-American and kept writing for the AFRO papers until his death.

events.title: Testimony publishes its premiere issue of African-American poetry
events.description: Volume I, Issue One of Testimony: A Journal of African-American Poetry appeared in Winter 1987 at $4.00, with a boxed 'Poetry of the 1980s' section listing 23 contributors including Rashidah Ismaili AbuBakr, Sandra West, and Nagueyalti Warren.

events.title: The Ridgewood News revives the memory of Alfred P. Smith
events.description: Tom Brady's retrospective, 'Newspaper of days ago remembered,' drew on David Steven Cohen's essay 'Alfred P. Smith: Bergen County's Latter-Day Ben Franklin' and included a photo portrait of Smith.

events.title: The Record profiles Smith as a civil rights writer
events.description: Joan Verdon's 'Second Look' column framed Smith as a publisher who editorialized against Southern lynchings and Englewood's school segregation policy.

events.title: Harry B. Webber dies in Newark at 90
events.description: Webber was city editor of the New Jersey Herald News, editor and publisher of the Newark magazine After Hours, and author of the 'Jersey Happenings' column for the Afro-American.

events.title: Rap Masters runs its November 1992 issue
events.description: The cover carries a full-bleed photograph of the Kris Kross duo with the red-and-yellow banner 'Exclusive! KRIS KROSS MINI-MAG!!' set directly above and overlapping it. Both readings are true of the same cover at once: Kris Kross is the dominant cover photograph and the banner advertises the mini-mag, so there is no internal conflict to resolve. The cover also carries 'Hip-Hop Style for the '90s', cover lines for Yo-Yo and Too Short, and a 'Who's Hot Now?' sidebar naming College Boyz, Pete Rock & CL Smooth, and Gang Starr. The bottom photo strip names Salt 'N Pepa, DMC, Queen Latifah, and MC Phlme.

events.title: The Sunday News calls The Landscape the nation's smallest newspaper
events.description: Nancy R. Peck's feature described Smith's 6-by-8-inch paper and dated the first issue to June 1882, twenty years of publication ending with his death in 1901. The article does not give his age at death; it quotes him 'at the age of 65, four years before his death in 1901,' which puts his age at death at 69, the same age The Record gives. The June 1882 start date differs from the May 1881 given in the 1987 and 1991 accounts.

events.title: A Trenton State College guide lists Utimme Umana/La Voz Oculta among 20 minority organizations
events.description: A September 27, 1993 Times article about TSC quotes 'the guide' saying the college has a minority scholarship program, a minority mentoring program and 20 minority organizations, 'including Utimme Umana/La Voz Oculta, the minority magazine.' The clipping never names the document as an orientation guide and never dates it, so it should not be called the fall 1993 orientation guide. The 'magazine' label is seventeen years after the paper was described as a weekly.

events.title: The Minority Business Development Agency is made permanent
events.description: A Nubian News editorial reports that President Biden signed the Bipartisan Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, which made the Minority Business Development Agency a permanent federal agency. Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo is named in the item. The log dates the signing only to November 2021.

events.title: Newark announces the 2022 National Black Political Convention
events.description: Newark Mayor Ras Baraka announced that the National Black Political Convention would return in 2022, to be held April 28-May 1, 2022 at the New Jersey Institute of Technology in Newark, fifty years after the 1972 Gary convention organized by his father Amiri Baraka, Sr. Jackson, Mississippi mayor Chokwe Antar Lumumba, jazz and R&B musician James Mtume, and NJIT president Joel Bloom joined the announcement. The log dates the announcement only to November 2021; the convention dates are as announced, not as held.

events.title: A Mercer County toy giveaway reaches families in Trenton
events.description: The Mercer CCYC gave toys to families with young children, working with West Trenton Toys for Tots and the US Marine Corps. The Nubian News covered it.

events.title: Trenton buries Christopher David, 17
events.description: The funeral service for Christopher David, 17, was held at the Ledford Home in Trenton. The Nubian News ran the obituary and quoted his mother, Brenda Meraz, who said he died after struggling with depression and bullying at school. The paper reports a suspected suicide; no official cause is given in the issue.

events.title: A Christmas Day arson fire kills a Trenton resident and burns six houses
events.description: A fatal fire set on the 200 block of Rusling St. at Division St. in Trenton on Christmas Day spread to six adjacent houses and to vehicles. The Nubian News covered it in English and Spanish, quoting community activist Luis González and resident Francisco Choc.

events.title: A suspect is charged with murder in the Trenton Christmas arson
events.description: The Mercer County prosecutor's office announced the arrest of Ronal Ordóñez Lima, 28, and charged him with murder in the Christmas Day Rusling St. fire.

events.title: A New Jersey bill would fund $5.15 million in school panic alarms
events.description: The Assembly Appropriations Committee introduced bill A-6258, allocating $5,150,531 for school security projects, chiefly panic alarms, statewide. Assemblyman Roy Freiman (D-Somerset, Mercer, Middlesex, Hunterdon) sponsored it. The Nubian News reported the introduction the next day.

events.title: The Nubian News publishes a 12-page bilingual issue as Vol. 6, No. 1
events.description: The January 7, 2022 issue runs 12 pages in English and Spanish out of Trenton, numbered Volume 6, No. 1. The masthead names Kamau Kujichagulia as publisher, Tanya Henry Turner as managing editor, Carlos Avila as El Latino News editor, Al Alatunji and Laura Lucia Rodriguez Pena as reporters, Karen Hilton as photographer, and Leslie Lauts and Vernon Daniels in circulation. The issue mixes local Trenton crime and community coverage with national editorials, book reviews, and 2021 obituaries. This is the only firsthand read of a contemporary New Jersey Black paper in the reading base.

events.title: A Newark Public Library program on Ollie Stewart is announced for May 23, 2023
events.description: A May 21, 2023 Daily Record column promoted an upcoming program, 'Fighting on Two Fronts: Black GIs in World War II and Ollie Stewart's Reporting in the NJ Afro-American,' led by Seton Hall historian Larry Greene and co-sponsored by NJPAC and the Newark History Society. The column promotes the program; it does not report that it was held. Savannah Wood, great-great-granddaughter of the paper's founder and manager of the AFRO archives, is quoted in the column and is not listed as a program participant.

events.title: The Newark Herald previews the NJ State Federation of Colored Women's Clubs convention at Bordentown
events.description: The July 16, 1938 Newark Herald ran an advance Society-page item, 'Women's Federation Meet In Bordentown / Elaborate Program Is Planned By Group,' by Claude Foster, datelined Bordentown, July 17. It reported that the Bordentown Manual Training School 'will be the scene of the twenty-third annual Convention of the New Jersey State Federation of Colored Women's Club ... to be held, July 20, 21, 22, and 23,' and printed the program in the future tense ('Dr. William R. Valentine, principal of Bordentown will deliver the welcoming address Wednesday evening'; 'THURSDAY MORNING, July 21'). The issue announces the convention; it does not report it as opened, and it does date the opening. The campus is the same one as the Ironsides Echo student paper.

events.title: Rev. Florence Randolph, pastor of Wallace Chapel, marks 45 years in the ministry
events.description: The July 4, 1942 New Jersey Herald News ran a Church Services page article headed 'Rev. Flor. Randolph Celebrates 45 Years In The Ministry' with a portrait captioned 'Rev. FLORENCE RANDOLPH'. The two facts come from one lede, not from separate mentions: 'SUMMIT - The 45th anniversary of Rev. Florence Randolph, pastor of Wallace Chapel AME Zion Church, is being celebrated beginning Tuesday past and continuing to July 8th.' The article does describe the observance: a multi-day program with Rev. E. S. Hardge presiding Wednesday, Rev. J. C. Nelson of Newark Thursday with a sermon by Rev. Walter R. Lovell of Charlotte, N. C., editor of the Star of Zion; Rev. Randolph presiding Sunday with Mrs. Rebecca Lassiter directing music; and Rev. Merrill D. Booker of Summit Monday, Rev. Murray Branch of Madison Tuesday, and Rev. O. C. Scott of Westfield on the closing night, Wednesday.
